projects.title: Northcote terrace, full rewire
projects.summary: A single-fronted 1890s terrace with four decades of additions behind the plaster. Documented before opening up, rewired, then documented again as built.
projects.demonstrationDisclosure: This record describes a fictional job created to demonstrate how work would be documented. It is not a completed project, the property does not exist, and no outcome, timeframe, cost or compliance claim here has been verified.

hero.alt: Orthographic elevation of a single-fronted terrace facade with the supply run from the meter box to the roof space marked in brass

story.heading: What the owners asked for
story.body: The owners had bought the house eighteen months earlier and had been adding lamps and extension leads to make rooms usable. They wanted to stop guessing which switch did what, and they wanted the work finished before the floors went down. Their actual question was not technical: they wanted to know whether the house was safe to leave children in.

story.heading: What we found behind the plaster
story.body: Three generations of wiring sharing one board: original rubber-insulated runs, a 1970s extension on its own circuit, and a kitchen addition fed from a socket circuit. Nothing was labelled and two circuits were bridged in a ceiling junction with no access hatch. We drew the existing arrangement before touching any of it, because the drawing is what makes the quote honest.

media.alt: Orthographic floor plan of the terrace with the existing lighting circuit traced in brass through four rooms, showing junctions and three ceiling fittings on drops

story.heading: How we sequenced it
story.body: We worked room by room from the rear so the family could keep the front of the house in use, and we kept the old board live until the new one was proven. Each circuit was terminated, tested and labelled before the next was pulled, which is slower on paper and considerably faster in practice than chasing faults at the end.

media.alt: Axonometric drawing of the roof space showing rafters and the new cable run pulled across the joists with junctions marked

story.heading: What went back on the wall
story.body: A replacement board with an RCBO per final circuit, each labelled to the room it serves rather than to a number nobody remembers. The old board was left in place, isolated and tagged, until the owners had lived with the new one for a fortnight.

media.alt: Close orthographic elevation of a single residual current breaker showing its label window, toggle, test button and terminations

story.heading: What the owners were left with
story.body: A drawing set showing both what was there and what is there now. If they sell, the next owner inherits the record. If they renovate again, nobody has to open a wall to find out what is behind it.

projects.title: Brunswick workshop, sub-main and supply
projects.summary: A detached brick workshop running off a domestic circuit it was never sized for. A new sub-main, its own board, and a trench drawn before anyone lifted a paver.
projects.demonstrationDisclosure: This record describes a fictional job created to demonstrate how work would be documented. It is not a completed project, the property does not exist, and no outcome, timeframe, cost or compliance claim here has been verified.

hero.alt: Site plan showing the dwelling, a detached workshop and the sub-main trench drawn between them with the meter position marked

story.heading: A workshop on an extension lead
story.body: The owner had been running a bench saw and a dust extractor from a socket circuit inside the house, via a lead through a window. Nothing had failed yet. That is usually the point at which someone calls, and it is the right time to call.

story.heading: Sizing it honestly
story.body: The interesting question was not the trench, it was the load. We measured what the tools actually draw when they start rather than what the plates claim, then sized the sub-main for the workshop the owner described wanting in five years, not the one standing there.

media.alt: Single-line schematic showing the supply, main switch, a busbar and eight final circuits terminating in lighting, socket and fixed-appliance symbols

story.heading: Where the trench went, and why
story.body: The shortest line crossed the only part of the garden the owner cared about. We took the longer route along the fence, which cost more in cable and less in goodwill, and drew it so the position is recoverable in twenty years when somebody wants to plant a tree.

story.heading: A workshop that is its own building
story.body: Its own board, its own protection, and a documented trench position. The window is closed.

media.alt: Drawn cable schedule plate: a ruled table of circuit rows with reference, description, rating and protection columns

projects.title: Kew renovation, lighting design and switching
projects.summary: A rear extension where the lighting had been laid out around the wiring rather than the rooms. Re-planned from the plan up, then wired to match the drawing.
projects.demonstrationDisclosure: This record describes a fictional job created to demonstrate how work would be documented. It is not a completed project, the property does not exist, and no outcome, timeframe, cost or compliance claim here has been verified.

hero.alt: Orthographic floor plan with the lighting circuit traced in brass across four rooms, showing junction positions and ceiling fittings on drops

story.heading: Switches in the wrong places
story.body: The extension was finished and the lighting worked, which is not the same as the lighting being right. Every switch was beside the door the electrician had reached first, and the kitchen bench was lit from behind whoever stood at it.

story.heading: Planning from the room, not the cable
story.body: We started from how each room is used and where people stand, marked the switch positions on the plan before any circuit was considered, and only then worked out how to reach them. This is the reverse of the usual order and it is the whole job.

media.alt: Vertical section through a stud wall showing the cable chase, studs drawn in hatch, and three outlet positions taken off the run

story.heading: Lighting that matches the room
story.body: Four lighting circuits, switching where people actually walk, and a plan that says why each position is where it is. The bench is lit from in front.
